pages.text: Ordinary glass, of sand, lime and potash, cracks when one side is hot and the other cold. For the laboratory Otto Schott made a glass of sand and borax: about 81% silica, 13% boric oxide, 4% soda and almost no lime. It expands a third as much as ordinary glass, so it takes a boiling flask, and acids do not touch it.$(br2)Only this glass makes a retort or a carboy.
pages.title: Why borosilicate

pages.text: One borax flux and two white sand make 4 $(thing)Borosilicate Glass Batch$().

Borax gives both the boron and the soda, so the batch has no lime and no potash. $(l:metalworking/flux)Borax flux$() is not the plain flux of the blast furnace, and it does not burn to lime.$(br2)The sand must be white, silica sand. Coloured sand has iron in it, and the glass would not be clear.

Borosilicate softens at about 820 °C and is worked from 1250 °C up to 1500 °C: hotter than that, TFC takes the glass off the pipe. A charcoal forge never gets there on its own draught (1000 °C), and one blower gives only 1204 °C. Two reach 1347 °C, and a $(l:metalworking/bellows)bellows$() 1600 °C.$(br2)Only a $(thing)ceramic$() blowpipe will serve. Brass melts at 930 °C, and a brass pipe refuses the batch, by hand and in the recipe. Sawing the glass off needs no heat.
pages.title: The heat and the pipe

pages.text: The $(thing)Glass Retort$(): blow, stretch, pinch with jacks, saw.
The $(thing)Glass Carboy$(): blow twice, roll with wool cloth, saw.

Borosilicate takes every acid of this book, hot, and a flask that boils. What it will not take is a steep gradient: above 550 °C a retort cracks, whatever is in it. Heat it through a $(l:tfcpp/acids#retort)sand bath$().$(br2)Glass breaks. A retort or a carboy lets out what it holds when it is broken, and an acid splashes. The use of both is in $(l:tfcpp/acids)Acids$().
pages.title: What it holds

pages.text: A $(thing)Glass Bulb$() is a pane of glass. It takes 5 mB of mercury (see $(l:tfcpp/sulfides#mercury)Sulfide Ores$()), for a thermometer or a manometer.
